implementation_notes: The metadata store is the class body: __tablename__ names the table and each Mapped[...] attribute with mapped_column(...) declares a column, its type and its options (primary_key, server_default, index, name as the first positional argument for a differently named column). The DeclarativeBase metaclass and its registry are the reader - they build a Table in the MetaData collection and a Mapper per class at import time - and the engine is SQLAlchemy's compiler plus unit of work, so the mapper code that would otherwise be written per class does not exist. Use imperative mapping when the class must not inherit from a framework base class, and Django's models when the application is a Django project, since migrations there are generated from the same declarations.
code_sketch:
class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column("user_name", String(64))
pitfalls: Two sources of truth are normal: migrations do not run from the declarative classes automatically, so the mapped metadata and the live schema drift until the two are compared.

Attribute name versus column name is easy to mix up: passing the column name positionally keeps the Python attribute different from the database column, and forgetting it produces 'column not found' at query time.
Mapped[...] annotations are validated against the type map, not the database, so an annotation that contradicts an existing column fails only when DDL or a query is compiled.

variants.name: SQLAlchemy imperative mapping (Table + map_imperatively)
variants.idiom_name: Core Table objects bound with registry.map_imperatively
variants.implementation_notes: Here the table is defined independently as a Core Table object - metadata as data rather than as class-body declarations - and the class is attached to it explicitly with registry.map_imperatively(User, user_table); the registry is the reader and the resulting Mapper is the same object the declarative form produces. It is the right tool when the mapped class already exists, when it must not inherit from a framework base class, or when one table has to be mapped differently in two systems, and it makes the metadata/engine boundary visible because the Table exists before the mapping is declared.
variants.code_sketch:
class User:                      # plain class, no framework base
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name

user_table = Table("users", metadata,
    Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True),
    Column("user_name", String(64)))
registry.map_imperatively(User, user_table)
pitfalls: Class and table must agree by hand: no annotation is checked, so a misspelled property creates an unused column and an AttributeError on load.
Mixing declarative and imperative configuration for the same class or table produces duplicate-registration errors that appear only when the second module is imported.

variants.name: Django models with the ModelBase metaclass
variants.implementation_notes: Django's metadata store is the class body too, but fields are explicit constructor calls (models.CharField(max_length=30, db_column="first_name")) collected by the ModelBase metaclass into the model's _meta options; the table name defaults to app_label plus model name and can be overridden in Meta. Because makemigrations generates the schema from the same metadata, the declared mapping and the database schema are intended to be one artifact, and the ORM compiler is the engine. Prefer it in Django projects where the admin, forms and migrations all consume the same declaration; the coupling to django.db makes it a poor fit for a standalone domain layer.
pitfalls: Model modules have import-time side effects against the app registry, so a model cannot be imported before Django is configured - which breaks naive layering.
Field changes require migrations: a db_column that no longer matches the database fails at query time with an opaque 'no such column'.
Querysets fetch lazily, so attribute access that looks cheap can execute SQL (the N+1 pattern) unless related columns are selected explicitly.
